question: How is ٱلَّذِى construed here?

positions.position: The relative is nominative as a subject or predicate of an omitted subject.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL [BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22#3/r2]: Fa-lā tajʿalū may coordinate a prohibition with worship, be subjunctive after an implied an, or depend on laʿalla so the sense is if you are mindful, do not make rivals; it may also be a prohibitive predicate of alladhī jaʿala. BAYDAWI-FULL [BAYDAWI-FULL:2:22/r1]: Alladhī may be a second adjective, an accusative or nominative expression of praise, or a subject whose predicate is the prohibition fa-lā tajʿalū; jaʿala itself can mean become or begin intransitively, bring into being with one object, or render with two. NASAFI-FULL [NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r13]: Alternatively, alladhī is a subject whose predicate is the prohibition; the fāʾ introduces the consequence implicit in the discourse: since God surrounded them with signs, they should not take partners. NASAFI-FULL [NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r2]: Alladhī may be accusative as a praise construction or nominative as the subject of an understood huwa. ABUHAYYAN-FULL [ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p156#2/r9]: The relative الذي جعل can be nominative or accusative; the nominative analyses continue in the next segment. ABUHAYYAN-FULL [ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p161/r11]: Another possible parse connects the prohibition to الذي, treated as the predicate of an omitted subject: he is the one who made these signs, so do not set up rivals. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22#3/r16]: If الذي is predicate of an omitted subject, the prohibition can attach to it: the signs testify to oneness, so no rivals should be assigned to God. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22/r7]: For رفع, the sounder analysis supplies a deleted subject: هو الذي جعل. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22/r8]: Another رفع analysis makes الذي the subject and فلا تجعلوا its predicate. ALUSI-FULL [ALUSI-FULL:v1p186/r6]: The long interruption objection can be eased by treating the following phrase as parenthetical, or by making الذي the subject with فلا تجعلوا as predicate; this parsing remains less likely despite al-Baydawi’s apparent preference. ALUSI-FULL [ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r3]: It may instead be nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject or as a subject whose predicate is فلا تجعلوا; the fāʾ can introduce a predicate after a past relative clause. ALUSI-FULL [ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r4]: Al-Akhfash allows an overt noun to serve as the linking pronoun in the relative construction; an imperative can be predicate through the standard interpretive account. ALUSI-FULL [ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r5]: Al-Alusi rejects the still more far-fetched proposal that الذي begins a clause whose predicate is رزقا لكم, understood with an omitted يرزق.

positions.position: The relative clause modifies the Lord or the preceding relative description.
positions.reasons: NAHHAS [NAHHAS:v1p197/r13]: The relative clause modifies the Lord or the preceding relative description. JISHUMI [JISHUMI:v1p281/r12]: The relative clause modifies the Lord or the preceding relative description. IBNATIYYA-FULL [IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p104#2/r11]: The relative clause modifies the Lord or the preceding relative description. ABUHAYYAN-FULL [ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r1]: An adjective may itself be modified only when it cannot agree directly with its described noun; the example is يا أيها الفارس ذو الجمة. ABUHAYYAN-FULL [ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r6]: The absence of a coordinating wāw before الذي keeps this and the prior description attached to one referent; conjunction would suggest a different referent. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22/r6]: An exception is made when something blocks the normal analysis; ذو الجمة in يا أيها الفارس ذو الجمة modifies الفارس.

positions.position: The relative can be detached in accusative praise or nominative as a new statement.
positions.reasons: NAHHAS [NAHHAS:v1p197/r14]: The relative can be detached in accusative praise or nominative as a new statement. KASHSHAF-FULL [KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p124#2/r2]: The relative can be detached in accusative praise or nominative as a new statement. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p93/r5]: The relative phrase alladhī jaʿala may be accusative as an adjective of the earlier alladhī or as praise; it may instead be nominative as a subject, likewise carrying praise. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p93/r6]: Alladhī introduces a known proposition to identify a singular referent; thus the verse presupposes that its audience knows who made earth a bed and heaven a structure. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p93/r7]: This presupposed recognition matches the claim that, when asked who created heaven and earth, the audience answers Allah.

positions.position: The relative is parsed as the object of tattaqūn.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL [ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r5]: Abū Ḥayyān calls Makki's further proposal to govern الذي by تتقون a gross parsing unworthy of the Qur'an. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22/r4]: Abu al-Baqāʾ begins with parsing الذي as the object of تتقون. ALUSI-FULL [ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r1]: الذي may be accusative as an adjective or apposition to ربكم, or detached with an implied verb of specification or praise; Abu al-Baqa’s analysis as object of تتقون is rejected as weak. ALUSI-FULL [ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r2]: Abu al-Baqa’s parsing of الذي as the object of تتقون is, in al-Alusi’s judgment, an unworthy and feeble analysis of the Qur’an.

positions.position: The relative is accusative as description, apposition, or praise.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL [ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r3]: The accusative can detach as praise or describe ربكم, the referent of الذي خلقكم; he prefers adjectives to modify the same noun unless impossible. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22/r1]: Of five accusative analyses for الذي, al-Samīn regards نصب على القطع as clearest. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22/r2]: Another accusative analysis makes الذي an adjective of ربكم. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22/r3]: Another accusative analysis makes الذي a بدل of ربكم. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22/r5]: A fifth analysis makes the relative adjective modify an adjective; normally adjectives do not themselves take adjectives unless an obstacle requires it.

positions.position: The proposed implicit 'I mean' or object of tattaqūn is rejected as weak.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL [IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p104#2/r12]: The proposed implicit 'I mean' or object of tattaqūn is rejected as weak. ABUHAYYAN-FULL [ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r4]: Abu Muhammad Makki allows the accusative by supplying أعني, but Abū Ḥayyān says the prior expression is unambiguous and needs no insertion.

positions.position: The relative can be a subject whose predicate is the prohibition.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL [ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r2]: Abu al-Hasan permits a repeated-subject construction using a person's alternate name; Abū Ḥayyān says Sibawayh disallows it. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22/r10]: The missing link can be supplied only by al-Akhfash's view that a repeated apparent name with the same referent links a clause, as in Zayd/AʿAbd Allāh.

positions.position: The subject-and-prohibition parsing faces grammatical objections.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22/r9]: Al-Samīn objects that its relative clause is past, unlike a conditional clause licensing فاء, and that the analysis lacks a linker.

question: What does جَعَلَ mean here, and what does it govern?

positions.position: Jaʿala means created, with the bed phrase treated as a circumstance.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI [JISHUMI:v1p281/r2]: Jaʿala means created, with the bed phrase treated as a circumstance. BAGHAWI-FULL [BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p72/r3]: Jaʿala means created, with the bed phrase treated as a circumstance. TABRISI [TABRISI:2:22/r3]: Jaʿala means created, with the bed phrase treated as a circumstance. QURTUBI-FULL [QURTUBI-FULL:2:22/r2]: Jaʿala can mean “created,” as in the verses about God’s creation of livestock categories and darkness and light. ABUHAYYAN-FULL [ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r8]: Others parse فراشا and بناء as circumstantial accusatives, treating جعل as “created” with one object and varying the verb for eloquence, as in 6:1. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22/r12]: If جعل means create, it governs الأرض alone and فراشا is a circumstantial accusative. ALUSI-FULL [ALUSI-FULL:v1p187#2/r9]: The clause beginning وأنزل coordinates with جعل; the first من marks origin and attaches to أنزل or introduces a fronted circumstantial phrase from the object, with fronting creating anticipation and cohesion or enabling the circumstantial reading. ALUSI-FULL [ALUSI-FULL:v1p187/r6]: جعل can mean ‘turned into,’ taking two objects, or ‘brought into existence,’ with the second accusative as a circumstantial phrase meaning the earth was created spread out for people. IBNASHUR-FULL [IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p332/r3]: If jaʿala means create, the blessing is the present condition of earth and sky; if it means transform, geological strata support their transition through stages, yielding blessings and signs in both their state and development, as in 21:30–32.

positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL [QURTUBI-FULL:2:22/r1]: Here jaʿala means “made” or “rendered,” since it governs two objects. QURTUBI-FULL [QURTUBI-FULL:2:22/r4]: Jaʿala can mean “took” or “began to,” as a poet says he made himself grow accustomed to a bite. NASAFI-FULL [NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r1]: Jaʿala means ‘made’ or ‘rendered.’ NASAFI-FULL [NASAFI-FULL:v1p26/r3]: Firāsh means a spread-out resting place for sitting, sleeping, and moving; it is the second object of jaʿala. ABUHAYYAN-FULL [ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p157/r7]: جعل means “made into,” taking الأرض and فراشا as two objects, with لكم attached to جعل. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22#3/r7]: On either meaning of تجعلوا it takes two objects: أندادا is first, and the preceding prepositional phrase is second and must precede it. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22/r11]: If جعل means make or render, it governs two objects: الأرض first and فراشا second. BURHAN [BURHAN:v4p130/r2]: A fourth sense of jaʿala is to transform something from one state into another; it takes two objects, as in physical transformations. BIQAI-FULL [BIQAI-FULL:v1p57/r11]: The verb jaʿala suggests a descent from one state to another, through which heedlessness settles over hearts. ITQAN [ITQAN:v2p469/r1]: Al-Raghib says ja‘ala is broader than fa‘ala and sana‘a: it can mean become, create, form one thing from another, make something take a state, or judge something to be so; 2:22 uses the state-making sense.

positions.position: Jaʿala means made or rendered and takes earth and bed as two objects.
positions.reasons: NAHHAS [NAHHAS:v1p197/r16]: Jaʿala means made or rendered and takes earth and bed as two objects. IBNATIYYA-FULL [IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p104#2/r13]: Jaʿala means made or rendered and takes earth and bed as two objects. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22/r13]: السماء بناء coordinates with الأرض فراشا under either analysis of جعل.

positions.position: Jaʿala can mean name or call.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL [QURTUBI-FULL:2:22/r3]: Jaʿala can mean “called” or “named,” as in calling the Qur’an Arabic and calling a share or gender for God.

positions.position: Jaʿala can be treated as an extra particle in some Arabic usages.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL [QURTUBI-FULL:2:22/r5]: Some treat jaʿala as an extra particle, supported by a poet who sees double because of old age and by a reported reading of 6:1.

question: What holds the earth steady as a bed?

positions.position: God keeps earth still and sustaining support ultimately depends on His will.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94#2/r1]: Against equal celestial pressure as earth's support, Rāzī asks why a pressure strong enough to hold it is not felt. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94#2/r10]: God's sustaining the unsupported heavens and earth is expressly affirmed in 35:41. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94#2/r11]: A useful bed cannot be excessively hard: walking or sleeping on stone hurts, while gold would impede cultivation, digging, and construction. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94#2/r12]: Earth also cannot be excessively soft, like water, into which feet would sink. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94#2/r13]: Earth cannot be transparent: light would not rest on it and it would not warm from sun and stars; God made it opaque and dusty so it warms and suits animals. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94#2/r14]: Earth must emerge from water; although its nature would sink and seas might cover it, God raised part like an exposed island for habitation. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94#2/r2]: The equal-pressure theory cannot explain why clouds and winds do not move in one fixed direction. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94#2/r3]: It cannot explain why motion toward the west is not easier than motion toward the east. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94#2/r4]: On this pressure theory, a heavier body should move more slowly because the restraining pressure acts more forcefully on it. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94#2/r6]: Aristotle and most followers say earth naturally seeks the celestial center; Rāzī calls this weak because bodies are equally corporeal and the differentiating property requires a freely choosing agent. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94#2/r7]: Abū Hāshim says upward tendencies in earth's lower half and downward tendencies in its upper half counterbalance to keep it still. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94#2/r8]: Rāzī objects that assigning opposite tendencies to the two halves requires a freely choosing agent, so it does not explain earth's rest independently of God. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94#2/r9]: After rejecting the proposed causes, Rāzī concludes that God alone makes earth stationary and cites His holding heaven and earth lest they depart. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94/r1]: For earth to serve as a bed, it must be still; Rāzī argues that a descending or rotating earth would frustrate ordinary jumping or travel. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94/r2]: If earth fell straight down, its greater weight would make it descend faster than a jumper; if it rotated east faster than a person moving west, the person could not reach a destination. Since people can move, it is still. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94/r3]: The claim that earth does not fall because it is limitless below is rejected: bodies have been proved finite. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94/r5]: The theory that celestial attraction pulls earth equally from all directions fails because it does not explain why smaller bodies are not pulled faster, or why upward-thrown dust returns. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p94/r6]: A fourth account attributes rest to equal pressure from all sides, like dust held at the center of a rapidly spun bottle.

question: What benefits and signs does the sky provide?

positions.position: The sky's light, form, contents, and motion provide benefits and show wisdom.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p98/r1]: Frequent mention of the heavens and earth in scripture signals their great importance and the immense secrets and wisdoms beyond human understanding. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p98/r2]: Heaven is adorned with seven things: lamps, moon, sun, Throne, Kursi, Preserved Tablet, and Pen; three are visible and four are known through revealed evidence. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p98/r3]: The Qur'an gives the heavens exalted names, then describes their end and their beginnings in detail; this attention shows their creation serves profound wisdom. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p98/r4]: The account of the heavens' beginning and dissolution supports the principle that God created the heavens, earth, and what lies between them for wisdom, not in vain. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p98/r5]: Heaven is the direction toward which hands rise in supplication and faces turn, and it is the source of light, clarity, purity, and freedom from corruption. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p98/r6]: Some describe heaven as active and earth as receptive; because an active cause is nobler than its recipient, this explains why heaven is usually mentioned first. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p98/r7]: Some say the plural heavens are needed for varied planetary conjunctions and changing angles of radiation, while one receptive earth suffices. question: What is the force of مِنَ ٱلثَّمَرَٰتِ?

SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22#2/r4]: من الثمرات attaches to أخرج and من is partitive. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22#2/r8]: Alternatively, من الثمرات is the object, meaning some water brings out some fruits; رزقا may then be حال meaning المرزوق. SAMIN-DURR [SAMIN-DURR:2:22/r18]: Alternatively من السماء attaches to an omitted element as a circumstantial phrase from ماء; a fronted modifier of an indefinite is construed as حال and partitive, with مياه omitted. ALUSI-FULL [ALUSI-FULL:v1p188/r10]: If the second min is partitive, some fruits remain ungrown; rizqan is a causal verbal noun for producing, and lakum is attached to rizq as its object. ALUSI-FULL [ALUSI-FULL:v1p189/r2]: The cited phrase “I harvested your garden's fruit” uses the feminine ending as an abstract unit, not a strictly singular unit. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p101#3/r12]: Min is partitive: some fruit becomes some of people's provision.

positions.position: Min explains the kind of provision produced.

RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p101#3/r13]: Min explains the kind of provision produced.

question: What accounts are reported for the origin of idol worship?

positions.position: Reports give different ancient, astral, commemorative, and Arabian origins for idol worship.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p103#2/r1]: Rāzī says no group asserts a fully equal partner with God in existence, power, knowledge, and wisdom. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p103#2/r10]: Another group held that planets were created by the greater God but create this world as intermediaries between God and humanity. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p103#2/r11]: Because planets were usually invisible, people made idols to represent them; over time they forgot the planets and worshipped only the statues. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p103#2/r12]: Astrologers prescribed talismans made at particular times in long cycles, believing them to bring benefits such as prosperity and protection; accumulated veneration became worship after the origin was forgotten. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p103#2/r13]: Another explanation is that people made images of revered deceased figures as intercessors with God on Judgment Day. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p103#2/r14]: Some may have treated idols as prayer niches, prostrating toward them as Muslims face the qibla; ignorant people later mistook this for worship of the idols. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p103#2/r15]: Some corporealists may have believed that God could indwell an idol and worshipped it on that interpretation. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p103#2/r2]: Dualists posit two gods: one mild and responsible for good, the other foolish and responsible for evil. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p103#2/r3]: The Sabeans say God created the planets, which administer the world; they worship them, while the planets worship God. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p103#2/r4]: Christians are another group that worships Jesus. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p103#2/r5]: Idol worship predates the earliest prophet whose history is known, Noah, and remains widespread; Noah's people already defended their idols. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p103#2/r6]: Since everyone knows a stone carved now did not create its worshipper or the heavens and earth, the durability of idol worship implies another motive. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p103#2/r7]: Abu Maʿshar says some Chinese and Indians imagined God and angels as beautiful bodies veiled in heaven, making attractive statues of them to seek closeness. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p103#2/r8]: Most scholars trace planet worship to people linking seasonal and worldly changes with the planets' positions and movements. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p103#2/r9]: One astrologically minded group regarded planets as self-existent beings that created the worlds and thus as gods in truth. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p105#2/r1]: Before Alexander, Greeks built temples to spiritual powers and luminous celestial bodies and worshipped them; several divine principles had round temples. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p105#2/r2]: Rāzī lists temples shaped as hexagons for Saturn, triangles for Jupiter, rectangles for Mars, and squares for the Sun. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p105#2/r3]: He adds that Venus's temple was triangular around a square, Mercury's triangular around a rectangle, and the Moon's octagonal. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p105#2/r4]: Historians say ʿAmr b. Luḥayy saw idol worshippers in al-Balqāʾ who called idols gods that brought victory and rain, received Hubal from them, and installed it in the Kaaba in Mecca, urging people to venerate it. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p105#2/r5]: Among famous idol shrines were Ghumdan in Sana'a, built by al-Dahhak for Venus and destroyed by Uthman, and Nawbahar in Balkh, built by Manūshahr for the Moon. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p105#2/r6]: Rāzī names Arab idols and their tribes or locations: Wadd for Kalb, Suwaʿ for Hudhayl, Yaghuth for Madhhij, Yaʿuq for Hamdan, Nasr for Dhu al-Kilaʿ in Himyar, al-Lat for Thaqif, Manat for Khazraj, al-ʿUzza for Kinana, and Asaf and Na'ila at Safa and Marwa. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p105#2/r7]: Qusayy and Zayd opposed idol worship; Zayd's poem rejects al-Lat and al-ʿUzza and asks whether one God or a thousand should be worshipped.

question: How is rational argument for faith defended?

positions.position: Prophets and scripture use reasoned proofs for oneness, prophethood, and resurrection.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p74#2/r3]: Al-Rāzī introduces the following verses as an argument establishing divine unity, prophethood, and resurrection. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r1]: After describing believers, unbelievers, and hypocrites, God shifts from speaking about them to addressing them directly, an iltifāt also seen in 1:5. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r2]: Direct address stirs and moves the hearer more than continuing to speak about that person in the third person. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r3]: The shift honors and draws the addressee near: after initially making the Messenger an intermediary, God now addresses the person without an intermediary. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r4]: The move from third to direct address suggests that a servant engaged in worship is continually ascending. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r5]: Because the earlier verses narrated their condition and these verses impose difficult commands, God’s direct personal address gives relief and makes the burden pleasant. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r6]: ʿAlqama and al-Ḥasan say that Qur’anic addresses “O people” are Meccan, while “O you who believe” is Medinan. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r7]: Al-Qāḍī accepts that distinction if it rests on transmitted reports, but rejects deriving it merely from the larger number of believers in Medina: believers may be addressed as people, and unbelievers may be commanded to worship just as believers are told to persist and increase in worship. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76#2/r1]: Ay connects the vocative to a noun bearing the definite article, just as dhū and alladhī connect generic nouns to descriptions and definite nouns to clauses; ay is ambiguous and needs a noun or equivalent adjective to specify it. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76#2/r2]: The vocative particle governs ay, while the following noun is its adjective, as in “O Zayd, the courteous”; unlike Zayd, ay cannot stand independently and therefore remains joined to its adjective and described noun. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76#2/r3]: The inserted attention particle reinforces the call and compensates for the genitive construction expected with ay. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76#2/r4]: The emphatic formula is frequent in the Qur’an because its commands, prohibitions, promises, threats, and momentous histories must awaken listeners who are heedless. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76/r1]: Words normally denote linguistic or nonlinguistic things; the vocative particle is different, functioning as an act that draws attention rather than denoting another thing. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76/r2]: “O Zayd” cannot mean “I call Zayd”: the latter is a truth-apt report, does not itself make Zayd the addressee, may be spoken to a third party, and reports rather than performs the call. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76/r3]: Though names are strongest and particles weakest, a name can join a particle in calling; by analogy, a human can serve the transcendent Lord through invocation and humble supplication. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76/r4]: Yā originally calls someone distant; hamza (a-) calls someone near. Using yā for someone nearby treats an inattentive or heedless person as distant. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p76/r5]: Although God is nearer than the jugular vein, a supplicant says “O Lord” either from humility and self-reproach, distancing himself from the stations of intimacy, or because answering prayer is supremely important. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p80/r10]: Rāzī turns to Qur’anic proofs of divine transcendence, maintaining that God is neither a body nor located in space. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p80/r4]: Rāzī identifies five proofs of the Creator in these verses: creating accountable people, their predecessors, heaven, earth, and fruits from rain sent down from heaven. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p80/r5]: The Qur’an’s other signs in the heavens and earth likewise aim to establish the Creator’s existence. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p80/r9]: Different fruits and animals arising despite shared four-element natures show that God is powerful and freely choosing, not acting by intrinsic necessity. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r1]: As evidence for transcendence, Rāzī cites God’s proof given to Abraham against his people. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r10]: When Pharaoh demanded another proof, Moses named the Lord of the East and West. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r11]: These proofs belong to the prophets’ practice: they reasoned them out and inherited them from their purified predecessors. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r12]: Moses also argued for his prophethood by offering a clear miracle as evidence of his truthfulness. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r13]: Muhammad’s argument for monotheism, prophethood, and resurrection is unmistakable because the Qur’an is full of such proofs. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r14]: The Qur’an refutes materialists who say only time destroys by presenting various proofs. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r15]: Varied plants and animals arising despite shared natural temperaments and celestial influences refute those who deny a freely choosing Creator. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r16]: Abraham’s argument when night covered him refutes those who make celestial bodies partners by claiming they influence the world. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r17]: The Qur’an also refutes lower partners: Christians claim divinity for Christ and idolaters for their idols. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r18]: One group denied prophethood altogether, asking whether God would send a human messenger. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r19]: Another group, including Jews and Christians, accepted prophethood in general but challenged Muhammad’s prophethood; the Qur’an answers their objections. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r2]: Abraham challenged his father’s worship of an idol that could neither hear, see, nor help him. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r20]: When critics objected to Qur’anic parables, God replied that He is not ashamed to give even a mosquito as an example. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r21]: When critics demanded further miracles, including a spring from the earth, the Qur’an answered their challenge. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r22]: When critics objected to gradual revelation as grounds for suspicion, God explained that it strengthened the Prophet’s heart. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r3]: Abraham verbally challenged his people about the statues to which they were devoted. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r4]: Abraham demonstrated the idols’ impotence by smashing them all except the largest, so that the people might turn to it. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r5]: Before the ruler, Abraham argued that his Lord gives life and death, exposing the ruler’s claim to do the same. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r6]: Rāzī says sound minds recognize that kalām merely presents these prophetic proofs and answers objections to them. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r7]: Abraham also asked God to show him how He revives the dead, addressing the afterlife. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r8]: Moses answered Pharaoh with the Lord who gave each thing its form and guidance, the same creation-and-guidance proof Abraham used of God creating and guiding him. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p81#2/r9]: Moses’ appeal to the Lord of Pharaoh’s forefathers echoes Abraham’s argument that his Lord gives life and death. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r1]: The Qur’an answers those who dispute resurrection with many proofs for the resurrection and against its deniers. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r10]: The Qur’an condemns arguing about God without knowledge, which implies that argument grounded in knowledge is not blameworthy and is praiseworthy. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r2]: To those who say obligations bring no benefit, God replies that good or evil deeds return to the doer. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r3]: To the claim that determinism invalidates obligation, God replies that He is not questioned about what He does, while people are questioned. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r4]: Rāzī abbreviates these examples because their full treatment appears elsewhere in the book. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r5]: Since every prophet practiced this discipline, Rāzī concludes that its critic is either an unbeliever or ignorant. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r6]: Rationally, taqlīd cannot justify choosing one authority: following everyone entails following unbelievers, choosing only some has no basis, and rejecting all imitation leaves rational inquiry. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r7]: Scripture commands calling to God with wisdom and good admonition and debating in the best manner; Rāzī interprets wisdom as proof and demonstration. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r8]: The commanded debate concerns monotheism and prophethood, not legal branches: such branches are pointless to those rejecting prophecy, while those accepting it would not dispute the Prophet. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p83/r9]: Because Muslims are commanded to follow Muhammad and take him as their example, they too must engage in the debate he was commanded to conduct. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p89#2/r10]: Celestial and elemental bodies share corporeality, so their differing quantities, shapes, and locations cannot be explained by corporeality or any property necessarily belonging to it. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p89#2/r4]: The possibility of attributes is inferred from the heavens and earth’s created arrangement; Rāzī specifically points to the earth as a resting-place and sky as a structure. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p89#2/r9]: Rāzī treats the earth and sky as cosmic evidence that natural bodies themselves depend on a maker; changes such as thunder, lightning, winds, clouds, and seasons are signs of the horizons.

positions.position: Human knowledge of remote celestial matters and the unseen is limited.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p101/r1]: Razi answers claims of detailed knowledge about remote celestial things by citing revelation that only God knows the unseen, human knowledge is limited, and the Prophet does not claim the unseen or God's stores. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p101/r2]: Humans cannot fully know their own essence and qualities, so they cannot claim detailed knowledge of the most distant things. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p101/r3]: An unnamed Arab poet says people may know today and yesterday but remain blind to what tomorrow holds. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p101/r4]: Labid says diviners using pebbles and bird omens do not know what God will bring about. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p101/r5]: Al-Jahiz compares the world to a prepared house: heaven is its roof, earth its carpet, stars its lamps, humans its steward, and plants and animals are arranged for their benefit. RAZI-FULL [RAZI-FULL:v2p101/r6]: Al-Jahiz says the world's order shows complete planning, comprehensive measure, profound wisdom, and unlimited power.
